title: SWE-Shift: Evaluating Coding Agents in Evolving Workspaces

Title:SWE-Shift: Evaluating Coding Agents in Evolving Workspaces
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Repository-level coding benchmarks largely assume that tasks and environments remain unchanged throughout execution. In software development, code, dependencies, runtime state, and requirements can change while an agent is still working. We introduce SWE-Shift, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents under such mid-execution changes. From the same saved history and workspace, a Clean continuation proceeds without intervention, while a matched Shifted continuation receives a task-relevant update. Success requires completing the current task, preserving still-valid work, and satisfying the applicable state and evidence checks. The benchmark contains 120 scenarios across 12 change families, each evaluated at nine scheduled intervention positions. We evaluate 17 coding-agent systems, all of which have lower Shifted than Clean success. GPT-6 Astra drops from 67.35% to 24.79%, with 20.34% paired success. Tool/session changes and stale evidence yield zero paired success across all systems. Late-position paired success is lower for some systems and higher for others. These results show that success on the unchanged task can coexist with failures to preserve work, recover state, or refresh evidence after an update.

report.summary: New benchmark SWE-Shift finds all 17 coding agents tested perform far worse when tasks or environments change mid-execution, exposing fragility behind static benchmark scores.
report.background: Repository-level coding benchmarks such as SWE-bench have traditionally measured agents on frozen snapshots: the task, dependencies, and runtime state stay fixed from start to finish. That makes scoring clean and reproducible, but it misrepresents real development, where requirements shift, dependencies upgrade, and teammates edit code while work is in progress. As coding agents moved from autocomplete to autonomous multi-step sessions, the gap between benchmark conditions and production conditions became a reliability question. A system that scores well on static tasks may silently discard valid work, act on stale information, or fail to recover tool state when the ground shifts. SWE-Shift, posted to arXiv in October 2026, targets exactly that gap by testing whether agents can adapt, not merely complete.
key_points: Paired design isolates disruption: each scenario runs twice from the same saved history and workspace, once as a Clean continuation and once as a Shifted continuation with a single task-relevant update injected at one of nine scheduled positions. Because the starting state is identical, score differences can be attributed to the change itself rather than task difficulty.

Every system degraded: all 17 coding-agent systems scored lower on Shifted runs. GPT-6 Astra fell from 67.35% to 24.79% success, with only 20.34% paired success, meaning in most runs it either failed the task outright or failed to preserve work or refresh evidence after the update.

Two failure families were total: tool/session changes and stale evidence produced zero paired success across every system tested. Agents could not re-establish tool state or invalidate conclusions drawn before the change, suggesting adaptation is largely absent rather than merely weak.

Timing effects differ by system: late-position updates hurt some agents more and others less, hinting at distinct strategies. Some re-plan readily early but lock in commitments late, while others keep revisiting work in ways that help or hurt depending on when the shift lands.

Success is three-part, not one: the benchmark requires completing the current task, preserving still-valid prior work, and satisfying applicable state and evidence checks. This exposes that a pass on the unchanged task can coexist with losing work, meaning headline pass rates overstate real robustness.
report.impact: For the AI industry, SWE-Shift reframes coding-agent evaluation from static task accuracy to change resilience, a capability that matters more as agents run longer sessions inside real repositories. Vendors will face pressure to report mid-run adaptation alongside standard pass rates. For developers, the results validate a common frustration: agents are brittle in messy, moving codebases, so expect more emphasis on checkpointing, re-planning, and evidence invalidation inside agent frameworks, plus diff-review workflows before commits. For regular users, the message is caution: assistants may silently undo work or act on outdated assumptions when a project changes, so products should surface change notifications rather than committing autonomously. The benchmark also gives buyers a concrete question to ask vendors about robustness.
report.tools: Follow SWE-Shift itself (arXiv 2610.32196) and its evaluation harness for replication. Related baselines worth studying include SWE-bench and SWE-bench Verified, plus open agent scaffolds such as SWE-agent, OpenHands, Aider, Cline, and Continue. For building change-resilient agents, look at frameworks with durable state and checkpointing, such as LangGraph persistence and Temporal-style workflow engines, and at diff-aware tooling like git worktrees for isolating experimental continuations.
